newsitem.title: USA: FDA panel votes against COR's intrifiban.
newsitem.headline: FDA panel votes against COR's intrifiban.

text.p: A Food and Drug Administration (FDA) advisory committee on Friday unanimously voted not to recommend COR Therapeutics' intrifiban (Integrilin) for treatment in certain heart conditions.

The panel said that the firm had provided insufficient data to support its contention that the clotbuster can reduce death, heart attack and other complications in patients getting percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty.
That procedure, which uses balloons, lasers, or shaving-type devices to clear blocked coronary arteries, is performed about 500,000 times a year in the United States.
COR only presented data from one clinical trial. FDA does not generally consider products for approval without data from two randomized, placebo-controlled studies.
The panel called the results of that trial positive, but said it wanted another study to confirm the first. Analysts had been generally skeptical that the drug would be recommended for approval.
Intrifiban, derived from the venom of a rattlesnake, prevents platelets from accumulating at injury sites, which is usually the cause of artery reclosure after angioplasty.

Patients receiving either a high or low dose of intrifiban in COR's pivotal IMPACT II trial had a decrease of 35-to-40 percent in abrupt artery closure, a major angioplasty complication that can from 24 hours to 30 days after the procedure.

While that result was impressive, COR said at the outset of the meeting that it had not satisfied its main trial goal -- a 33 percent reduction in death, heart attacks, and the need for urgent intervention in the first 30 days after treatment. Instead, patients had a decrease of beteween 14 and 22 percent.

But, fewer patients getting intrifiban died than those taking placebo. About seven percent of placebo patients died, while 5.5 percent of intrifiban patients died. That 1.5 percentage point reduction was seen at 48 hours, 30 days, and six months after patients had angioplasty. All patients in the trial also received a blood thinner, heparin, and aspirin, in addition to intrifiban.
COR applied for FDA approval in April 1996, in a worldwide marketing partnership with Schering-Plough Corp.
If approved, Intrifiban would be a rival to Eli Lilly and Co's abciximab (Reopro), which was approved in 1995 for high-risk angioplasty patients.
Oppenheimer & Co. biotechnology analyst Matthew Geller says that if approved, intrifiban could see sales of $400-to-500 million a year.
Merck & Co and Roche Holding Ltd are also developing platelet inhibitors, and results from their studies are expected in 1998.
